# CiFn durable root-job dispatch checkpoint

2026-10-20. Extends the encrypted-record checkpoint with atomic prepared dispatch
intent, transport retry and durable single-winner assignment. This is not
exactly-once execution or a complete durable scheduler.

## Acceptance and state transitions

API, signed webhook and cron creation use `prepareRun()` before any run is stored.
It snapshots the input, resolves all job environments and redaction values, and
computes root jobs from the DAG. Preparation errors leave no accepted run or
queued message. `DatabaseStore.createPreparedRun()` inserts the run, original
normalized definition, redaction values and root-job intents in one encrypted
record/write. The existing memory store remains supported, without a durability
claim. Run creation does not provide an HTTP idempotency key; repeated create
requests can still create separate runs.

A dispatch identity is `JSON.stringify([runId, jobKey, 1])`. Attempt 1 is the only
supported execution attempt in this checkpoint. Publication retries retain this
identity; they do not create execution attempts. Each intent has `ready` or
`claimed` state. Queue payloads include `dispatchId`; assigned payloads also
include an opaque `claimToken`.

Publication uses a revision-CAS lease with a random token and 5-second expiry.
Only its holder can acknowledge publication. A failed enqueue is retried after
5 seconds; an acknowledged but unclaimed delivery is eligible again after
30 seconds. A crash between enqueue and acknowledgement therefore permits
duplicate transport messages. The transport lease is not an execution lease and
never authorizes reassignment of claimed work. Server clocks must be synchronized
for publication scheduling; assignment uniqueness is enforced by database CAS.

The server publisher scans one bounded page of 100 queued/running records per
1-second tick and advances a cursor across pages. Initial acceptance also tries
publication immediately. Queue/publication failures emit generic diagnostics and
leave durable intent available; a transient queue failure does not turn an
already committed run into a failed creation response. Embedders using
`createApp()` must start its returned `dispatchPublisher` and await `stop()`
before closing their adapter. The built server does this automatically.

An authenticated runner heartbeat consumes transport messages and atomically
claims only an eligible pending job from a nonterminal run. The database record,
not the transport payload, supplies the returned job/environment and verifies
its runner label. CAS persists runner identity, claim token and timestamp,
promotes job and run to running, then returns the payload. Competing heartbeats
or duplicate messages cannot return a second assignment. Each request drains at
most 100 stale/duplicate messages. A failed database claim returns failure and
leaves intent ready; later publication recovers a destructively dequeued message.
Cancelled and terminal runs cannot be newly claimed or republished.

## Restart and compatibility

Restart replays only ready intents whose delivery/publication interval has
elapsed. A claimed job remains claimed even if the runner or HTTP response was
lost. `getDispatchStates(runId)` exposes privileged reconciliation metadata
without job environments or secret values. There is no implicit timeout,
requeue, lease renewal, claim-resume endpoint or operator reassignment command.

The encrypted payload extension is backward compatible and requires no DDL
change. Existing records created without prepared intents remain readable and
are not automatically dispatched. Durable-mode heartbeat ignores legacy queue
messages without `dispatchId`; migration of those runs requires explicit
reconciliation. This avoids silently rerunning jobs whose prior execution is
unknown. Generic `createRun()` remains a record-only API; use `prepareRun()` plus
`acceptRun()` for dispatch.

## Validation

Real SQLite tests cover atomic intent/redaction persistence, delivery failure and
close/reopen retry, duplicate messages through authenticated HTTP heartbeats,
competing publisher leases, expired leases, stale acknowledgement tokens,
cancellation, and preparation failure across API/webhook/cron. A native SQLite
trigger rejects claim updates after destructive dequeue: no assignment is
acknowledged, and retry succeeds after the database failure is removed.

The built-server acceptance creates two runs, claims one job, kills the process
with SIGKILL and restarts with the same database/key and an empty memory queue.
The queued job is republished and claimed within the bounded probe; the previously
claimed job is never reassigned. Runner authentication and encrypted record
checks remain part of the probe. It uses real elapsed time, real HTTP, the native
SQLite binding and the built entrypoint, and cleans its child processes/files.

Commands from the repository root:

```sh
npm test --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run lint --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run test:durable --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
node cifn/typescript/control-plane/scripts/verify-module-consumers.mjs
node cifn/typescript/control-plane/scripts/verify-startup.mjs
```

## Remaining original gates

- Remote runner claim acknowledgement/resumption, step/job completion protocol,
  authenticated claim-token validation on completion, execution leases/fencing,
  explicit retry policy and reassignment. Response loss after committed claim
  deliberately leaves work for reconciliation rather than risking duplicate
  side effects. The existing local runner still directly mutates MemoryStore;
  it is not a completed remote durable runner integration.
- Atomic dependent-job scheduling and terminal run/notification outboxes.
  This checkpoint prepares root jobs only. Completion, cancellation delivery,
  downstream DAG execution and provider-side idempotency remain open.
- FlowFn live acceptance, transport duplicate retention/backpressure, prolonged
  queue failures and hung provider requests, clock skew, large-scale scan cost,
  and the original dispatch/read/parse performance targets. Unclaimed work may
  have multiple transport copies; queue capacity and retention must accommodate
  them. The 30-second redelivery interval is not a measured 5-second recovery SLA.
- Other language, CLI/dashboard, provider, migration/key rotation, installed
  package, deployment, backup/restore and security/load gates from the original
  specification remain unchanged. No production deployment was performed.
EOF

# CiFn durable remote shell execution checkpoint

2026-10-20. Adds a functioning remote shell runner to the durable control plane.
It supersedes the root-only/no-completion limits in the earlier dispatch
checkpoint for newly prepared runs. Production readiness remains incomplete.

## Protocol and durable state

All jobs now have an encrypted prepared payload captured at run acceptance.
Root intents start ready; dependent intents start blocked. Their environment and
secret snapshot is retained rather than reconstructed or re-resolved when a
predecessor completes.

The existing authenticated heartbeat offers a durable claim. Three bounded JSON
endpoints use the registered runner secret, not an application API key:

- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/resume`: `runnerId`, optional pagination cursor.
  Returns only that runner's outstanding claims and their prepared payloads.
- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/ack`: `runnerId`, `runId`, `dispatchId`,
  `claimToken`, `executionId`. CAS binds an execution identity before work starts.
  Repeating the same acknowledgement is safe; competing identities conflict.
- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/complete`: the same identity plus `result` with a
  terminal job status and the exact ordered step keys/terminal statuses.

Completion requires the runner binding, claim token and acknowledged execution
identity. Invalid authentication returns 401, malformed shape 400, stale or
conflicting identity/result 409, and a storage failure 503. Server-observed
completion timestamps are assigned internally. A canonical result digest makes
identical retries return the same `{accepted:true}` receipt without applying a
second transition; a conflicting result is rejected.

One run-row CAS commits completion, step/job statuses, dependent-intent promotion
and the resulting run status. An already ready/claimed/completed intent cannot
be scheduled again. Concurrent parent completions can release a join only once.
Failed dependencies skip blocked descendants; independent branches may finish.
A run becomes terminal only when all jobs are terminal. Cancelled runs reject
new execution acknowledgements and completions that were not already committed.
Notifications are not made durable by this transition.

The payload's `dispatchProtocolVersion:2` marks fully prepared runs. Earlier
record-only or root-only payloads remain readable but are not automatically
published/claimed by this execution protocol. Old claims without protocol
metadata are reconciliation-only. There is no automatic migration or unsafe
secret re-resolution for historical records; reconcile them explicitly before
creating replacement work.

## Runner lifecycle and secret handling

The built runner requires `CIFN_CONTROL_PLANE_URL`, `CIFN_RUNNER_ID`,
`CIFN_RUNNER_SECRET` and an explicit persistent `CIFN_RUNNER_STATE_DIR`.
`CIFN_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` defaults to 1000 (minimum 10). The control plane must use
the durable SQLite store for these endpoints. MemoryStore remains available for
local execution, not remote durability.

The runner reuses the existing Runner and shell executor with an ephemeral
per-job projection. That projection drives actual subprocess execution and
collects results; it is not the durable authority. Only shell `run` steps are
supported by this remote checkpoint. Image/container jobs and provider `uses`
steps fail explicitly. Existing local execution/provider paths remain available
and separately tested.

Before acknowledging a claim, the runner saves only identity/execution metadata
in its journal. It fsyncs an exclusive started marker before invoking the shell,
then durably saves terminal statuses before sending completion. Journal files
use mode 0600, the directory mode 0700, atomic replacement and directory fsync.
The journal contains no raw job environment, commands, log output, provider
credentials or runner secret. It retains scoped claim/execution tokens and
terminal statuses. Resume re-fetches payloads through runner authentication.

On restart:

- Unacknowledged offers and prepared journal entries may be resumed.
- A saved completed result is resent, never re-executed.
- A started marker without a saved result is uncertain. The runner emits a
  generic reconciliation diagnostic and refuses automatic re-execution.
- An execution acknowledged elsewhere cannot be adopted with a new identity.

The exclusive started marker also prevents two local processes using one journal
from spawning the same execution. This protects against duplicate execution
caused by protocol/journal retries; it does not claim exactly-once external side
effects or recover an unknown result after a process/host loss.

Full-job logging was removed. Shell jobs receive prepared job variables plus a
small base environment (PATH/LANG/TMPDIR), not the runner's control-plane
credentials. Results saved/reported by this path contain statuses only, so raw
stdout/stderr and secret values cannot enter the journal. Existing executor
redaction is retained for its in-memory logs. This is not an OS/container sandbox.

## Validation

Real SQLite protocol tests exercise owner/runner/token binding, acknowledgement
retries, competing execution owners, wrong step results, duplicate/conflicting
completion, cancelled execution, prepared-secret preservation across reopen,
and parallel-parent join promotion. A native SQLite trigger rejects completion:
no partial result or downstream promotion is committed, and a later retry works.

`verify-remote-execution.mjs` starts the built control plane and runner as separate
processes. A real shell build writes a witness file, followed by a dependent test.
It loses the initial offer, resumes it, drops a successfully committed completion
response, kills the control plane with SIGKILL, and restarts on the same SQLite
file. The saved result is retried and the dependent job executes once. It checks
final step/job state after another reopen, rejects a forged completion token,
and verifies witness contents rather than inferring execution from records.

The probe then kills the runner process group after a real shell side effect but
before result persistence. Restart with the same journal leaves the job uncertain
and does not repeat the side effect. It checks private journal modes and scans
journal/process output for fixture secrets. Child processes, SQLite files,
journals and witness files are removed afterward.

Reproduce after installing the control-plane, runner and existing TestFn workspace
closure and building shared DB dependencies:

```sh
npm test --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm test --workspace=./cifn/typescript/runner
npm run lint --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run lint --workspace=./cifn/typescript/runner
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/runner
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
```

Validation is local Node 20.20.0/native SQLite evidence. The existing runner suite
also exercises local executor paths; it is not evidence that provider steps are
supported remotely.

## Remaining original gates

Execution lease expiry/renewal, explicit operator reconciliation/reassignment,
crash recovery after an unknown subprocess result, durable notification delivery,
remote step/log streaming, artifact/cache/checkout/TestFn/HostFn/Docker provider
integration, and step-level secret expressions remain open. Remote shell jobs
with unsupported providers fail rather than claiming success. Cancellation does
not terminate a running subprocess. Completion is reported per job, so step
progress before terminal completion is not durably streamed.

Journal retention/backup and filesystem portability, installed tarball/runtime
matrices, live FlowFn/SecFn/FileFn/LogFn/SendFn acceptance, distributed load and
performance targets, production deployment, Python/CLI/dashboard parity and the
remaining original specification requirements are not completed by this slice.
EOF

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
```

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)

2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
```

# AGENTS.md - AI Agent Development Guide for Superfunctions

> **Purpose**: This document provides AI agents with essential information for working effectively on the Superfunctions monorepo.

## 🏗️ Repository Structure

Superfunctions is a **Turbo monorepo** containing self-hosted developer tools and libraries. The repository is organized into:

### Core Functions (Top-Level Directories)

Individual superfunction packages, each providing specific developer capabilities:

- **`authfn/`** - Authentication & API key management
- **`cachefn/`** - Multi-tier caching with function memoization
- **`drawfn/`** - Cross-framework drawing canvas for brainstorming
- **`plugfn/`** - Integration platform (OAuth, webhooks, 75+ providers)
- **`searchfn/`** - Browser-first full-text search with IndexedDB
- **`secfn/`** - Security functions (secrets vault, rate limiting, monitoring)
- **`testfn/`** - Testing utilities and frameworks
- **`botfn/`** - Bot framework (Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations)
- **`hostfn/`** - Hosting and deployment utilities
- **`uifn/`** - UI components and utilities
- **`watchfn/`** - File watching and monitoring
- **`billfn/`** - Billing and payment processing
- **`browsefn/`** - Browser automation utilities
- **`chartfn/`** - Charting and visualization
- **`datafn/`** - Data processing utilities
- **`docsfn/`** - Documentation generation
- **`filefn/`** - File operations and management
- **`flowfn/`** - Flow control (queues, streams, workflows)
- **`iconfn/`** - Icon utilities
- **`logfn/`** - Logging utilities
- **`mailfn/`** - Programmable real inboxes for products, agents, and tests
- **`sendfn/`** - Email/messaging utilities

### Shared Packages (`packages/`)

Framework-agnostic core libraries used across superfunctions:

**TypeScript Packages:**

- `@superfunctions/http` - HTTP abstractions
- `@superfunctions/http-express` - Express.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-fastify` - Fastify adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-hono` - Hono adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-next` - Next.js adapter
- `@superfunctions/http-sveltekit` - SvelteKit adapter
- `@superfunctions/db` - Database adapter system (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- `@superfunctions/auth` - Authentication abstraction layer
- `@superfunctions/cli` - CLI tool for schema management

**Python Packages:**

- `superfunctions` (from `python-core/`) - Core namespace package
- `superfunctions-sqlalchemy` (from `python-sqlalchemy/`)
- `superfunctions-fastapi` (from `python-fastapi/`)
- `superfunctions-flask` (from `python-flask/`)

### Other Directories

- **`_conduct/`** - Root-level artifacts for shared code (implementation plans, specs, audits)
- **`21n/`** - Organization-specific packages
- **`.agent/`** - Agent workflows and automation
- **`.github/`** - GitHub Actions and CI/CD

## 📦 Package Naming Conventions

### Rule A: Shared Packages Format

**Any package shared across superfunctions uses `@superfunctions/{name}` format**

Examples:

```
packages/db/          → @superfunctions/db
packages/http/        → @superfunctions/http
packages/auth/        → @superfunctions/auth
packages/cli/         → @superfunctions/cli
```

### Rule B: Core Function Packages Format

**Single-package functions**: Use simple name without scope

```
authfn/ts-sdk/        → authfn
drawfn/core/          → drawfn
cachefn/typescript/   → cachefn
plugfn/core/         → plugfn
searchfn/             → searchfn
```

**Multi-package functions**: Use `@{functionname}/{sub-package}` format (if needed in future)

```
@authfn/core          (example for future multi-package structure)
@authfn/providers     (example for future multi-package structure)
```

**Current Status**: All core functions currently use single-package structure. The scoped format is reserved for future expansion if a function needs multiple published packages.

### Rule C: Monorepo Structure

**The root `superfunctions` is a Turbo monorepo. Avoid nested monorepos.**

- ✅ Use subfolders to organize functions (e.g., `authfn/python/`, `authfn/ts-sdk/`)
- ❌ Do NOT create nested monorepos (e.g., `authfn/` should NOT be another monorepo)
- ✅ Use Turbo workspaces defined in root `package.json`

Current workspaces:

```json
{
  "workspaces": [
    "searchfn",
    "botfn/*",
    "hostfn/*",
    "authfn/*",
    "packages/*",
    "21n/*"
  ]
}
```

### Rule D: Artifact Location

**Create artifacts (`.md` files) in `.conduct` folders**

- **Function-specific artifacts**: `{function}/.conduct/`
  - Examples: `authfn/.conduct/implementation.md`, `drawfn/.conduct/audit_report.md`
- **Shared/root artifacts**: `_conduct/`
  - Examples: `_conduct/implementation.md`, `_conduct/spec.md`

Artifact types:

- `implementation.md` - Implementation plans
- `spec.md` - Technical specifications
- `audit_report.md` - Code audits and reviews
- `task.md` - Task tracking
- `walkthrough.md` - Feature walkthroughs

## 🗂️ Language Support

Most core functions support **both TypeScript and Python**:

### TypeScript Structure

```
{function}/
├── typescript/       or  core/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── package.json
│   ├── tsconfig.json
│   └── vitest.config.ts
```

### Python Structure

```
{function}/
├── python/
│   ├── {function}/        # Python package directory
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   └── ...
│   ├── tests/
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── README.md
```

### Examples

- `authfn/typescript/` + `authfn/python/`
- `cachefn/typescript/` + `cachefn/python/`
- `secfn/typescript/` + `secfn/python/`
- `plugfn/core/` + `plugfn/python/`
- `drawfn/core/` (TypeScript only, with React/Svelte adapters)
- `searchfn/` (TypeScript only, browser-focused)

## 🔧 Development Workflow

### Building

```bash
# Build all packages
npm run build

# Build specific package (from root)
turbo run build --filter=authfn
turbo run build --filter=@superfunctions/db

# Build from package directory
cd authfn/ts-sdk && npm run build
```

### Testing

```bash
# Test all packages
npm test

# Test specific package
turbo run test --filter=drawfn

# Watch mode
npm run test:watch
```

### Linting

```bash
npm run lint
```

### Package Manager

- **npm** (v10.2.0+) - Specified in `packageManager` field
- Uses npm workspaces for monorepo management
- Turbo for build orchestration

## 🎯 Key Superfunctions Features

### AuthFn

- Multi-provider authentication (OAuth, API keys, JWT)
- Framework-agnostic with adapters for Express, Fastify, Hono, Next.js, SvelteKit
- Database-agnostic (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely)
- TypeScript + Python SDKs

### DrawFn

- Cross-framework drawing canvas
- React and Svelte adapters
- Scene management, export capabilities
- Tolerant parsing with version validation

### PlugFn

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### MailFn

- Stable and expiring programmable inboxes
- Cloudflare Email Workers, D1, R2, and Queues deployment adapter
- Raw MIME and attachment evidence, waits, OTP/link extraction, threads, labels, and search
- Typed client, test helpers, CLI, MCP server, custom domains, webhooks, and SendFn composition
- Scoped credentials, retention, audit, quotas, and explicitly gated public-platform controls

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts

## 🔍 Finding Code

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.

Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

cat > cifn/.conduct/cancellation-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# CiFn remote shell cancellation checkpoint

2026-10-20. Extends the remote execution checkpoint without changing the original
production-readiness requirements. No shared packages or dependencies changed.

## Contract

The application-authenticated run cancellation endpoint still commits
`run.status=cancelled`. That commit is cancellation intent, not proof that work
has stopped. New bounded JSON runner endpoints use the registered runner secret
and the complete `{runnerId,runId,dispatchId,claimToken,executionId}` identity:

- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/status` returns only `cancelRequested`, `completed`
  and `stopped`. It checks the claim owner/token and, once bound, execution ID.
- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/stopped` CAS-records a server timestamp on a
  cancelled claim. Repeating the same receipt is safe; another execution identity
  or a completed claim conflicts. No environment or secret payload is returned.

Before acknowledgement and before creating the started marker, the runner
checks cancellation. A cancellation racing acknowledgement is observed after
the acknowledgement conflict. During execution it polls once per second, with
at most one status request in flight and a ten-second request timeout. A failed
request is not cancellation; during an outage work may continue to its existing
five-minute command timeout. There is no guaranteed one-second cancellation SLA.

Each remote shell command runs in an owned POSIX process group with asynchronous
output capture capped at 1 MiB. Cancellation sends SIGTERM, allows one second,
then sends SIGKILL if the group remains. The runner checks group disappearance
for up to five more seconds. Shell exit or closed stdio alone is insufficient.
A remaining or inaccessible group causes uncertain execution, not a stopped
receipt. The same cleanup handles timeout, output overflow, and background
children left behind when a shell exits. A command leaving background children
is considered failed. Group signalling uses only the currently spawned child's
identity; no PID is read from a journal. Later steps check the abort signal and
do not execute after observed cancellation.

Once its owned group has disappeared, the runner durably writes a `cancelled`
journal phase before reporting stopped. A lost response is retried after journal
reopen without execution. Run cancellation and successful completion use the
same run-row CAS: whichever commits first determines acceptance. A completion
receipt committed before cancellation remains replayable, including when another
job in the same run is subsequently cancelled. Cancellation metadata does not
invent new job/step enum values; the cancelled run retains its last durable job
snapshot and the claim stores the stopped receipt.

## Evidence

- Native SQLite close/reopen tests cover runner/token/execution binding, cancel
  before acknowledgement, idempotent stopped receipts, completion/cancel races,
  and replay of a previously committed result after run cancellation.
- Runner tests cover cancellation before acknowledgement, racing acknowledgement,
  before start, no spawn with an already aborted signal, receipt response loss,
  and transient observation failure without false cancellation.
- An actual shell test starts a SIGTERM-resistant descendant, confirms escalation
  stops it, checks that the next step did not run, and keeps an unrelated process
  alive. It uses real subprocesses rather than injected executor success.
- The built two-process HTTP acceptance probe now cancels an executing job,
  confirms its resistant descendant's process group returns ESRCH before a
  durable stopped receipt, checks no late/next-step witness, preserves an
  unrelated sentinel, and rejects a forged stopped token. Existing SQLite
  restart, DAG execution, lost offer/completion, and uncertain execution tests
  remain in the same probe. It explicitly cleans up the separate uncertain
  shell group after killing the runner, without asking the restarted runner to
  adopt or signal it.

Reproduce with package tests/typechecks and:

```sh
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/runner
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
```

## Remaining original gates

This is POSIX process-group control, not an OS sandbox. Processes deliberately
escaping their group/session, Windows process trees, abrupt host/runner death,
and an unconfirmed process-group kill require operator reconciliation. A
restarted runner never signals historical PIDs or reexecutes uncertain work.
SIGTERM to the runner itself still requests shutdown after the current tick;
it is not an authenticated run-cancellation operation.

Execution leases/reassignment, notification outbox and SendFn delivery, provider
steps, remote logs/progress/artifacts, live provider acceptance, installed
consumer/runtime matrices, performance/deployment and Python/CLI/dashboard
parity remain open as recorded in the original spec and execution checkpoint.
EOF

# CiFn remote shell cancellation checkpoint

2026-10-20. Extends the remote execution checkpoint without changing the original
production-readiness requirements. No shared packages or dependencies changed.

## Contract

The application-authenticated run cancellation endpoint still commits
`run.status=cancelled`. That commit is cancellation intent, not proof that work
has stopped. New bounded JSON runner endpoints use the registered runner secret
and the complete `{runnerId,runId,dispatchId,claimToken,executionId}` identity:

- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/status` returns only `cancelRequested`, `completed`
  and `stopped`. It checks the claim owner/token and, once bound, execution ID.
- `POST /api/v1/runners/claims/stopped` CAS-records a server timestamp on a
  cancelled claim. Repeating the same receipt is safe; another execution identity
  or a completed claim conflicts. No environment or secret payload is returned.

Before acknowledgement and before creating the started marker, the runner
checks cancellation. A cancellation racing acknowledgement is observed after
the acknowledgement conflict. During execution it polls once per second, with
at most one status request in flight and a ten-second request timeout. A failed
request is not cancellation; during an outage work may continue to its existing
five-minute command timeout. There is no guaranteed one-second cancellation SLA.

Each remote shell command runs in an owned POSIX process group with asynchronous
output capture capped at 1 MiB. Cancellation sends SIGTERM, allows one second,
then sends SIGKILL if the group remains. The runner checks group disappearance
for up to five more seconds. Shell exit or closed stdio alone is insufficient.
A remaining or inaccessible group causes uncertain execution, not a stopped
receipt. The same cleanup handles timeout, output overflow, and background
children left behind when a shell exits. A command leaving background children
is considered failed. Group signalling uses only the currently spawned child's
identity; no PID is read from a journal. Later steps check the abort signal and
do not execute after observed cancellation.

Once its owned group has disappeared, the runner durably writes a `cancelled`
journal phase before reporting stopped. A lost response is retried after journal
reopen without execution. Run cancellation and successful completion use the
same run-row CAS: whichever commits first determines acceptance. A completion
receipt committed before cancellation remains replayable, including when another
job in the same run is subsequently cancelled. Cancellation metadata does not
invent new job/step enum values; the cancelled run retains its last durable job
snapshot and the claim stores the stopped receipt.

## Evidence

- Native SQLite close/reopen tests cover runner/token/execution binding, cancel
  before acknowledgement, idempotent stopped receipts, completion/cancel races,
  and replay of a previously committed result after run cancellation.
- Runner tests cover cancellation before acknowledgement, racing acknowledgement,
  before start, no spawn with an already aborted signal, receipt response loss,
  and transient observation failure without false cancellation.
- An actual shell test starts a SIGTERM-resistant descendant, confirms escalation
  stops it, checks that the next step did not run, and keeps an unrelated process
  alive. It uses real subprocesses rather than injected executor success.
- The built two-process HTTP acceptance probe now cancels an executing job,
  confirms its resistant descendant's process group returns ESRCH before a
  durable stopped receipt, checks no late/next-step witness, preserves an
  unrelated sentinel, and rejects a forged stopped token. Existing SQLite
  restart, DAG execution, lost offer/completion, and uncertain execution tests
  remain in the same probe. It explicitly cleans up the separate uncertain
  shell group after killing the runner, without asking the restarted runner to
  adopt or signal it.

Reproduce with package tests/typechecks and:

```sh
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/runner
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
```

## Remaining original gates

This is POSIX process-group control, not an OS sandbox. Processes deliberately
escaping their group/session, Windows process trees, abrupt host/runner death,
and an unconfirmed process-group kill require operator reconciliation. A
restarted runner never signals historical PIDs or reexecutes uncertain work.
SIGTERM to the runner itself still requests shutdown after the current tick;
it is not an authenticated run-cancellation operation.

Execution leases/reassignment, notification outbox and SendFn delivery, provider
steps, remote logs/progress/artifacts, live provider acceptance, installed
consumer/runtime matrices, performance/deployment and Python/CLI/dashboard
parity remain open as recorded in the original spec and execution checkpoint.
EOF

text(await tools.exec_command({cmd:"cat > cifn/.conduct/notification-outbox-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# CiFn durable webhook notification checkpoint

2026-10-20. Implements the webhook delivery portion of SPEC §7.3. Email/SendFn
provider delivery and per-pipeline notification configuration remain open.

## Configuration and integration

The built control plane requires durable SQLite storage when notifications are
enabled. Configure:

```sh
CIFN_NOTIFY_ON_RUN_COMPLETE=true
CIFN_NOTIFICATION_WEBHOOK_URL=https://receiver.example/cifn-events
```

The flag accepts only `true` or `false`; default is disabled. Enabled configuration
without an explicit HTTP(S) webhook fails startup. Userinfo/fragments and
non-HTTP protocols are rejected. Redirects are not followed. Email configuration
(`CIFN_NOTIFICATION_EMAIL_TO`) fails explicitly while enabled; the old
`EmailSendFnClient` no longer logs and returns fabricated success.

Programmatic durable callers may supply `DatabaseStoreOptions.notifications` or
`createApp({store,sendFnConfig:{enabled:true,webhookUrl}})`. The durable app returns
`notificationPublisher`; embedding applications must start/stop it, as the built
server does. Injected `sendFn` callbacks are rejected for durable stores because
they bypass this delivery contract. MemoryStore's existing callback interface
remains a best-effort local/testing path and is not durable delivery evidence.

The destination is snapshotted into each run's encrypted state at acceptance.
Changing configuration applies to subsequently accepted runs; it does not reroute
or erase pending events. Disabling new notifications does not discard already
accepted delivery obligations. Historical runs without the snapshot produce no
retroactive event. Configuration must be consistent across accepting replicas.

## Atomic event and delivery semantics

The first terminal run transition creates one event inside the same encrypted
run-row CAS. This includes remote DAG completion, direct terminal status updates,
and cancellation. A failed update commits neither transition nor intent. Repeated
completion/cancellation and stopped receipts do not create additional events.

Event IDs are stable SHA-256 identities over namespace, run ID, terminal status
and protocol version. Payloads include `eventId`, `runId`, terminal `status`,
`pipelineRef`, trigger type, timestamps and a fixed summary. Raw trigger payload,
commands, environments, logs and prepared credentials are excluded. Known secret
values are redacted from pipeline references, URL userinfo/query/fragment are
removed, and reference strings are capped. Destinations remain encrypted at rest
and are never printed in failure diagnostics.

A `cancelled` event means cancellation intent committed. Its summary explicitly
states that subprocess termination is tracked separately. It does not claim that
jobs stopped, change completion semantics, or replace claim stopped receipts.

The publisher scans ten terminal records per bounded tick and advances a cursor.
It CAS-claims each pending event with a random token and a ten-second lease. HTTP
POST uses a three-second timeout and includes both `Idempotency-Key` and
`X-CiFn-Event-Id` headers. Only a 2xx response followed by a matching, unexpired
lease acknowledgement records delivery. Failed requests, non-2xx responses and
expired leases preserve pending work. Retry delay doubles from one second and
caps at sixty seconds; retries are not silently discarded after an attempt cap.
An expired lease can be reclaimed after process failure; stale workers cannot
acknowledge a newer lease. Shutdown waits for the active bounded publisher tick.

Delivery is **at least once**. A receiver may accept a request whose response is
lost, or before CiFn crashes while recording its receipt. The same event ID is
retried and the receiver must deduplicate it. A 2xx response means receiver HTTP
acceptance, not downstream email delivery or exactly-once effects. No generic
remote SendFn API was invented; a real SendFn email/provider integration still
needs its documented SDK and transaction-status semantics.

## Evidence

Native SQLite tests cover atomic terminal/outbox rollback with an actual trigger,
close/reopen, concurrent publisher claims, expired/forged/stale lease rejection,
stable event identity, retry backoff, delivered-event suppression, disabled and
invalid configuration, and explicit failure of the email placeholder. Real HTTP
tests return 503, accept then drop a response, retry after database reopen with
receiver deduplication, and never return headers to verify the request timeout.

`verify-notifications.mjs` starts the built control plane as a subprocess and a
real HTTP receiver. It drives authenticated completion, observes failed delivery
and accepted response loss, SIGKILLs the control plane, reopens the same SQLite
file, verifies replay with one receiver identity, retries completion, delivers a
cancellation-intent event, and verifies disabling new events does not emit one.
It scans SQLite/output for fixture secrets and cleans children, sockets and files.
This probe exercises notification delivery, not shell execution; the separate
remote execution probe proves real shell/DAG/cancellation behavior.

```sh
npm test --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run lint --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm exec --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane -- tsc -p tsconfig.durable.json
npm run test:notifications --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
```

## Remaining original gates

Email via the actual SendFn SDK/provider, per-pipeline notification options,
provider credentials/rotation, operator dead-letter/retry tooling, retention,
large-history scan/index performance and deployed receiver/provider acceptance
remain incomplete. Memory notification callbacks are not made durable. Existing
execution lease/reconciliation, remote provider/log/artifact, platform/runtime,
Python/CLI/dashboard, load/performance and deployment gates remain open.
EOF

With SQLite storage, set `CIFN_NOTIFY_ON_RUN_COMPLETE=true` and

`Idempotency-Key`; receivers must deduplicate retries. Cancellation events do not
assert that subprocesses stopped. Enabled email configuration fails explicitly
until a real SendFn email integration is supplied. See the
[notification outbox contract](.conduct/notification-outbox-readiness.md).
''';p.write_text(s)

# CiFn durable webhook notification checkpoint

2026-10-20. Implements the webhook delivery portion of SPEC §7.3. Email/SendFn
provider delivery and per-pipeline notification configuration remain open.

## Configuration and integration

The built control plane requires durable SQLite storage when notifications are
enabled. Configure:

```sh
CIFN_NOTIFY_ON_RUN_COMPLETE=true
CIFN_NOTIFICATION_WEBHOOK_URL=https://receiver.example/cifn-events
```

The flag accepts only `true` or `false`; default is disabled. Enabled configuration
without an explicit HTTP(S) webhook fails startup. Userinfo/fragments and
non-HTTP protocols are rejected. Redirects are not followed. Email configuration
(`CIFN_NOTIFICATION_EMAIL_TO`) fails explicitly while enabled; the old
`EmailSendFnClient` no longer logs and returns fabricated success.

Programmatic durable callers may supply `DatabaseStoreOptions.notifications` or
`createApp({store,sendFnConfig:{enabled:true,webhookUrl}})`. The durable app returns
`notificationPublisher`; embedding applications must start/stop it, as the built
server does. Injected `sendFn` callbacks are rejected for durable stores because
they bypass this delivery contract. MemoryStore's existing callback interface
remains a best-effort local/testing path and is not durable delivery evidence.

The destination is snapshotted into each run's encrypted state at acceptance.
Changing configuration applies to subsequently accepted runs; it does not reroute
or erase pending events. Disabling new notifications does not discard already
accepted delivery obligations. Historical runs without the snapshot produce no
retroactive event. Configuration must be consistent across accepting replicas.

## Atomic event and delivery semantics

The first terminal run transition creates one event inside the same encrypted
run-row CAS. This includes remote DAG completion, direct terminal status updates,
and cancellation. A failed update commits neither transition nor intent. Repeated
completion/cancellation and stopped receipts do not create additional events.

Event IDs are stable SHA-256 identities over namespace, run ID, terminal status
and protocol version. Payloads include `eventId`, `runId`, terminal `status`,
`pipelineRef`, trigger type, timestamps and a fixed summary. Raw trigger payload,
commands, environments, logs and prepared credentials are excluded. Known secret
values are redacted from pipeline references, URL userinfo/query/fragment are
removed, and reference strings are capped. Destinations remain encrypted at rest
and are never printed in failure diagnostics.

A `cancelled` event means cancellation intent committed. Its summary explicitly
states that subprocess termination is tracked separately. It does not claim that
jobs stopped, change completion semantics, or replace claim stopped receipts.

The publisher scans ten terminal records per bounded tick and advances a cursor.
It CAS-claims each pending event with a random token and a ten-second lease. HTTP
POST uses a three-second timeout and includes both `Idempotency-Key` and
`X-CiFn-Event-Id` headers. Only a 2xx response followed by a matching, unexpired
lease acknowledgement records delivery. Failed requests, non-2xx responses and
expired leases preserve pending work. Retry delay doubles from one second and
caps at sixty seconds; retries are not silently discarded after an attempt cap.
An expired lease can be reclaimed after process failure; stale workers cannot
acknowledge a newer lease. Shutdown waits for the active bounded publisher tick.

Delivery is **at least once**. A receiver may accept a request whose response is
lost, or before CiFn crashes while recording its receipt. The same event ID is
retried and the receiver must deduplicate it. A 2xx response means receiver HTTP
acceptance, not downstream email delivery or exactly-once effects. No generic
remote SendFn API was invented; a real SendFn email/provider integration still
needs its documented SDK and transaction-status semantics.

## Evidence

Native SQLite tests cover atomic terminal/outbox rollback with an actual trigger,
close/reopen, concurrent publisher claims, expired/forged/stale lease rejection,
stable event identity, retry backoff, delivered-event suppression, disabled and
invalid configuration, and explicit failure of the email placeholder. Real HTTP
tests return 503, accept then drop a response, retry after database reopen with
receiver deduplication, and never return headers to verify the request timeout.

`verify-notifications.mjs` starts the built control plane as a subprocess and a
real HTTP receiver. It drives authenticated completion, observes failed delivery
and accepted response loss, SIGKILLs the control plane, reopens the same SQLite
file, verifies replay with one receiver identity, retries completion, delivers a
cancellation-intent event, and verifies disabling new events does not emit one.
It scans SQLite/output for fixture secrets and cleans children, sockets and files.
This probe exercises notification delivery, not shell execution; the separate
remote execution probe proves real shell/DAG/cancellation behavior.

```sh
npm test --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run lint --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm exec --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane -- tsc -p tsconfig.durable.json
npm run test:notifications --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
npm run test:remote --workspace=./cifn/typescript/control-plane
```

## Remaining original gates

Email via the actual SendFn SDK/provider, per-pipeline notification options,
provider credentials/rotation, operator dead-letter/retry tooling, retention,
large-history scan/index performance and deployed receiver/provider acceptance
remain incomplete. Memory notification callbacks are not made durable. Existing
execution lease/reconciliation, remote provider/log/artifact, platform/runtime,
Python/CLI/dashboard, load/performance and deployment gates remain open.

- Self-hosted integration platform
- 75+ provider integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord, Linear, Stripe)
- OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- Webhook support
- Multi-tenant with secure token storage

### SearchFn

- Browser-first full-text search
- IndexedDB persistence with in-memory LRU cache
- BM25 scoring
- FlexSearch-compatible API
- Worker-ready with snapshot export/import

### MailFn

- Stable and expiring programmable inboxes
- Cloudflare Email Workers, D1, R2, and Queues deployment adapter
- Raw MIME and attachment evidence, waits, OTP/link extraction, threads, labels, and search
- Typed client, test helpers, CLI, MCP server, custom domains, webhooks, and SendFn composition
- Scoped credentials, retention, audit, quotas, and explicitly gated public-platform controls

### CacheFn

- Multi-tier caching (memory, IndexedDB, external)
- Function memoization
- TTL and invalidation strategies
- Browser and server support

### SecFn

- Secrets vault management
- Access control and permissions
- Rate limiting
- Security monitoring
- Secret scanning

### BotFn

- Multi-platform bot framework
- Discord, GitHub, Linear integrations
- Shared types and persistence layer
- Event-driven architecture

## 🛠️ Common Tasks

### Adding a New Function

1. Create top-level directory: `{functionname}/`
2. Add TypeScript SDK: `{functionname}/typescript/` or `{functionname}/ts-sdk/`
3. (Optional) Add Python SDK: `{functionname}/python/`
4. Create `.conduct/` for artifacts
5. Add to workspace in root `package.json`
6. Package name: `{functionname}` (not scoped unless multi-package)

### Adding a Shared Package

1. Create in `packages/{name}/`
2. Package name: `@superfunctions/{name}`
3. Add to workspace (already covered by `packages/*`)
4. Update dependent packages

### Creating Artifacts

1. Function-specific: `{function}/.conduct/{artifact}.md`
2. Shared/root: `_conduct/{artifact}.md`
3. Use consistent naming: `implementation.md`, `spec.md`, `audit_report.md`, etc.

### Working with Turbo

```bash
# Run task across all packages
turbo run build
turbo run test

# Run for specific package
turbo run build --filter=authfn

# Run with dependencies
turbo run build --filter=authfn...

# Clear cache
turbo run clean
```

## 📚 Important Files

### Root Configuration

- `package.json` - Workspace and script definitions
- `turbo.json` - Turbo build configuration
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript base config (if exists)

### Package Configuration

- `package.json` - Package metadata, dependencies, scripts
- `tsconfig.json` - TypeScript configuration
- `vitest.config.ts` - Test configuration
- `pyproject.toml` - Python package configuration

### Documentation

- `README.md` - Package overview and usage
- `SPEC.md` - Technical specification (common in larger functions)
- `.conduct/*.md` - Implementation plans, audits, tasks

## 🔍 Finding Code

### Search Patterns

- **Function implementations**: `{function}/typescript/src/` or `{function}/python/{function}/`
- **Tests**: `__tests__/`, `tests/`, `*.test.ts`, `test_*.py`
- **Types**: `types.ts`, `models.py`, `src/types/`
- **Adapters**: `packages/http-*/`, `packages/python-*/`, `adapters/`
- **Examples**: `examples/`, `{function}/examples/`

### Key Directories

```
superfunctions/
├── {function}/              # Core function packages
│   ├── typescript/          # TS implementation
│   ├── python/              # Python implementation
│   ├── .conduct/            # Artifacts
│   ├── README.md            # Documentation
│   └── SPEC.md              # Specification (if exists)
├── packages/                # Shared packages
│   ├── {name}/              # @superfunctions/{name}
│   └── python-{name}/       # Python shared packages
└── _conduct/                # Root artifacts
```

## 🚀 Best Practices

### Super functions ecosystem (Very important)

- Reuse shared packages from `packages/` folder like http abstraction, db abstraction, etc.
- Never duplicate shared code like http adapters, db abstractions, etc.
- Don't reexport http-adapters etc - end consumers of the core function package will use the adapters directly. Refer `authfn` implementation for usage of core http router, core db, http adapters and db interface usage.
- Function packages that accept a `@superfunctions/db` `Adapter` must wrap the incoming adapter internally with their own schema, for example `wrapWithSchema(config.database, getSchema(...))`, before passing it to services/storage. Do not require app consumers to pass `adapterSchema` to `drizzleAdapter`, `kyselyAdapter`, `prismaAdapter`, or `memoryAdapter`; `adapterSchema` is a deprecated compatibility escape hatch for direct app-level adapter use.

### Code Organization

- Keep shared code in `packages/`
- Keep function-specific code in `{function}/`
- Use TypeScript for type safety
- Provide Python SDKs for backend-focused functions
- Write comprehensive tests

### Documentation

- Update README.md with usage examples
- Create SPEC.md for complex functions
- Document breaking changes
- Keep artifacts in `.conduct/` folders

### Testing

- Use Vitest for TypeScript
- Use pytest for Python
- Maintain high test coverage
- Test adapters separately

### Versioning

- Follow semantic versioning
- Coordinate versions across language SDKs
- Document migration guides for breaking changes

## 🔗 Related Resources

- **Repository**: https://github.com/21nCo/super-functions
- **License**: MIT (most packages) / Apache-2.0 (some packages)
- **Organization**: 21n
- **Contact**: hello@21n.org

## 📝 Notes for AI Agents

1. **Always check both TypeScript and Python** implementations when working on core functions
2. **Respect the naming conventions** - shared packages use `@superfunctions/`, functions use simple names
3. **Create artifacts in `.conduct/` folders**, not in root or arbitrary locations
4. **Avoid nested monorepos** - use subfolders within the main Turbo monorepo
5. **Use Turbo commands** for cross-package operations
6. **Check existing patterns** in similar functions before implementing new features
7. **Maintain consistency** across TypeScript and Python SDKs
8. **Update workspaces** in root `package.json` when adding new packages
9. **Follow existing test patterns** (Vitest for TS, pytest for Python)
10. **Document thoroughly** - this is a developer-focused ecosystem

---

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-10
**Monorepo Version**: 0.1.0
**Package Manager**: npm@10.2.0
**Build Tool**: Turbo v2.0.0

{"cmd":"cat > cachefn/.conduct/memoize-sync-readiness.md <<'EOF'
# Populated memoizeSync hit performance

2026-10-20. The synchronous TypeScript memoizer previously scanned every cached
entry for expiry before every lookup, including caches with no TTL. A warmed
single-key benchmark did not expose the resulting population-dependent hit cost.

## Behavior

A lookup now checks expiry only for the requested key and updates its LRU order
on a live hit. Hits do not renew TTL. An expired key is removed and recomputed at
the exact `now >= expiresAt` boundary; expiration does not count as eviction.
Undefined values remain cacheable. No TTL and `Infinity` retain their existing
non-expiring behavior, and zero capacity still prevents caching.

Cold expired entries are reclaimed when an insertion needs capacity and when
`stats()` requests an exact live-entry count. Capacity cleanup occurs after the
wrapped function returns, so expiry during a slow computation and entries added
by recursive calls are accounted for before evicting a live LRU entry. The cache
remains bounded by `maxSize`. Clear/delete controls and statistics retain their
existing contracts. No expiry queue, timer, or secondary retention structure was
introduced.

A live hit performs one expiry check plus amortized constant-time Map operations,
independent of population apart from key generation and occasional engine Map
maintenance/GC. A full-cache miss and `stats()` still scan O(n) entries. This
checkpoint does not claim constant-time insertion or cleanup. Lazy expiry is
consistent with SPEC and V0_SPEC; expired values are never returned just because
physical cleanup is deferred.

## Tests

Dedicated cases cover an expired MRU entry alongside a live LRU entry, exact TTL
boundaries and undefined values, cold-entry statistics, expiry during computation,
recursive cache filling, 1,000 non-expiring entries, delete/clear, and immediate
expiry. The existing synchronous/async memoization tests also pass.

```sh
npm test -w @cachefn/core -- --run __tests__/memoize.test.ts __tests__/memoize-sync-expiry.test.ts
npm run typecheck -w @cachefn/core
npm test -w @cachefn/core
```

Results at this checkpoint: 18 focused memoization tests; 231 full TypeScript
tests; production and public type-contract checks passed. Concurrent core registry
changes have separate evidence and are not included in this implementation claim.

## Populated browser benchmark

`scripts/memoize-sync-benchmark.mjs` measures actual synchronous calls, without
`await` or baseline subtraction. Each case seeds 1, 1,000 or 10,000 entries,
warms 2,000 round-robin hits, then measures 20,000 further round-robin hits. It
covers default argument hashing and a custom key generator, each with no TTL and
a finite one-hour TTL. Assertions verify population, computations, hit counts and
zero eviction, so an empty or repeatedly recomputed cache cannot pass as a hit
benchmark. The original V0 memoization target remains <0.1 ms; reported pass uses
p99, consistent with the existing browser benchmark.

The harness can load the memoizer from a Git revision without modifying the
working tree. Output records the exact memoizer source SHA256, revision/working
source selection, host, browser, timer resolution, statistics and checksum.
Other source dependencies come from the current checkout.

```sh
export PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE_PATH=/path/to/playwright
export BROWSER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/path/to/chrome
node cachefn/typescript/scripts/memoize-sync-benchmark.mjs --label=before --ref=fe5b036d035cf76616514d5360237acdbdd0a50e
node cachefn/typescript/scripts/memoize-sync-benchmark.mjs --label=after
```

Local acceptance used Apple M4 Pro / macOS Darwin 27 arm64, Node 20.20.0 and real
Chrome 154.0.8037.58. Cross-origin isolation was enabled; observed timer resolution
was approximately 0.005 ms. Raw outputs are [before](memoize-sync-before.json)
and [after](memoize-sync-after.json).

| 10,000-entry case | Before p99 (ms) | After p99 (ms) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Custom key, no TTL | 0.055 | 0.005 |
| Custom key, finite TTL | 0.060 | 0.005 |
| Default key, no TTL | 0.060 | 0.005 |
| Default key, finite TTL | 0.065 | 0.005 |

All 12 after cases met the original 0.1 ms target on this host. The baseline also
met it for these populations; the correction removes its per-hit linear scan,
not a claimed target failure. After p99 is at the timer's resolution: these
numbers do not establish nanosecond precision, a universal speedup factor, or
performance on other hardware. Maximum latency and means remain in the raw
outputs so percentile reporting does not hide outliers.

## Remaining original gates

Full-cache miss/cleanup performance, arbitrary key/payload sizes, other browser
engines and deployment environments are not established by this hit benchmark.
Native Safari and Firefox acceptance remains separate. Python was inspected but
not changed: its synchronous memoizer still scans for expiry; this TypeScript
checkpoint is not Python performance evidence. Original full-SPEC capabilities,
packaging/provider/browser/runtime and broader readiness gates retain their
existing scope; no single benchmark establishes complete production readiness.
EOF

# Local flag prerequisites and environment overrides

2026-10-20. Implements the local prerequisite/environment portions of the original
UserFn specification's Flag model, SDK and Feature Flags sections. It extends
local bootstrap without claiming a configuration server, signed/ETag delivery,
background refresh or exposure transport.

## Configuration contract

TypeScript adds `FlagPrerequisite { key, expectedValue }`, optional
`FlagConfig.prerequisites`, `FlagEnvironmentOverride`, optional
`FlagConfig.environmentOverrides`, and `UserFnOptions.environment`. Python exposes
`FlagPrerequisite(key, expected_value)`, `FlagEnvironmentOverride`,
`FlagConfig.prerequisites`, `FlagConfig.environment_overrides`, and
`UserFnOptions.environment`. These are native SDK configuration types; this
checkpoint does not introduce a general camelCase/snake_case wire codec.

Every prerequisite must be available and its evaluated value must equal the
expected JSON value. Objects compare without key-order dependence; arrays remain
ordered; booleans, strings and numbers remain distinct. False, zero, empty strings,
arrays and objects are valid expected values. Python numeric comparison uses
finite float/IEEE-754 representation to match JavaScript JSON numbers, with
OverflowError/nonfinite rejection. Native Python arbitrary-precision integers
are outside shared exact numeric precision; encode exact large IDs as strings.
Tests distinguish the safe-integer boundary and confirm JavaScript rounding above
it. No string-to-number or boolean-to-number coercion is performed.

Missing, disabled, unmet and cyclic dependencies make the requested flag
unavailable: `getFlag/get_flag` returns that call's supplied fallback, not the
flag's configured default or a dependency's fabricated fallback. For example,
a missing dependency cannot satisfy `expectedValue: false`. This is not a forced
boolean false return: applications must choose an appropriate fallback for gated
features. Unrelated valid flags remain available. All prerequisites are ANDed.

Evaluation uses iterative DFS with per-call outcomes and cycle detection. It is
independent of definition insertion order and does not recurse through dependency
chains; 5,000-node chains are covered. Each dependency sees the same current user
and environment, and no outcome cache survives across users, identity resets,
configuration replacements or calls. Existing segments, inline constraints,
ordered rules, anonymous-user behavior and rollout percentage logic remain in
place. Environment is not added to the hash salt; a user's existing bucket stays
stable when an environment changes the percentage.

Environment names are exact, case-sensitive, nonempty strings. Missing/unknown
environments inherit the base flag. Only own TypeScript mapping entries are used,
including literal `__proto__` names; inherited `constructor`/`toString` entries
are never overrides. Overrides may replace `enabled`, `defaultValue`,
`defaultVariationId`, and the complete ordered rule array. Omitted fields inherit;
empty rule arrays explicitly replace base rules. Null/None for an override's
default variation explicitly clears it. Python uses an internal omission sentinel
to distinguish omitted default value/variation from explicit values; normal
construction does not require importing the sentinel. Base default variations
continue to take precedence unless replaced/cleared.

Base `enabled: false` remains a global kill switch: environment `enabled: true`
cannot resurrect it. An environment can additionally disable a globally enabled
flag. Variations and prerequisites are shared; overrides cannot remove dependency
gates or invent a second variation namespace.

## Validation and mutation boundaries

Definition replacement validates before modifying evaluator state. Invalid
replacements raise TypeError and preserve prior definitions. Duplicate/empty keys,
malformed prerequisite/override structures, unknown variation references,
out-of-range/nonfinite rollouts, unsupported constraint operators, cyclic JSON,
nonfinite values and unsupported value objects are rejected explicitly. Cycles or
missing nodes in the flag dependency graph are different: they are allowed to load
but resolve unavailable, supporting incomplete configurations without accidental
enablement. Known segment operators are preserved.

Loaded definitions are snapshotted. Modifying input objects after `setFlags` does
not change evaluation, and returned structured flag values are copied so they
cannot alter future prerequisite decisions. Caller-supplied fallback objects
retain their existing caller-owned behavior. Segments keep their existing
configuration contract; this change is not a general segment parity rewrite.

Operator save and enable-toggle paths use the same definition validator before
storage. The admin flag input/output schema now includes prerequisites,
environment overrides and the preexisting defaultVariationId field. Save, list
and global enable-toggle preserve them without dropping configuration. Tests use
the actual injected memory operator store and environment scope; this is not
proof of durable flag configuration storage. Shared dispatcher schemas are
validated explicitly; direct adapter invocation also reaches domain validation.

## Dependency and package closure

`@userfn/admin` now depends on the current shared `@superfunctions/admin` 0.1.5,
using local `@mcpfn/core` 0.0.6. A scoped npm workspace install and local builds
provided the actual dependencies. The root lock change is limited to the UserFn
admin dependency and removal of its obsolete nested admin/MCP/AJV graph; unrelated
npm optional/dev metadata churn was discarded. No shared source was changed.

A fresh installed CJS type consumer exposed the SDK's existing unconditional ESM
`types` export. Main and operator exports now select `.d.ts` for import and
`.d.cts` for require, matching the already generated runtime formats.

## Acceptance evidence

- TypeScript SDK source tests, production typecheck, CJS/ESM and declaration build.
- Python 3.9 source tests, plus a fresh built wheel installed in an isolated
  Python 3.12 environment; copied tests run against site-packages, without source
  pythonpath injection.
- Shared Unicode hash vectors and end-to-end environment-rollout prerequisites
  in both SDKs, including non-BMP and lone-surrogate IDs/keys. The separate
  [hash migration note](flag-hash-parity-readiness.md) documents changed Python
  non-BMP assignments; unchanged assignments are not claimed.
- Actual admin save/list/toggle and schema acceptance/rejection tests, typecheck
  and build with the local shared dependency closure.
- `typescript/scripts/verify-flag-context.mjs` packs SDK, UserFn admin, shared admin
  and MCP; installs all four tarballs in a fresh directory with normal dependency
  resolution; exercises ESM SDK/admin and CJS SDK runtime; then compiles installed
  `.mts` and `.cts` consumers under strict NodeNext without skipLibCheck or peer
  bypass. Temporary consumers are removed after the run.

Reproduce SDK/admin checks after building MCP/shared admin prerequisites:

```sh

npm test --prefix userfn/typescript
python3 -m pytest userfn/python/tests -q
npm run build --prefix userfn/typescript
npm test --prefix userfn/admin
npm run typecheck --prefix userfn/admin
npm run build --prefix userfn/admin
node userfn/typescript/scripts/verify-flag-context.mjs
```

## Remaining original requirements

Durable flag/config service storage, authenticated publish/fetch, signing and
ETag refresh, automatic refresh scheduling, exposure delivery, evaluation
telemetry, feature-flag UI/hooks, broader segment parity/operators, flag owner/tag
administration and deployed/browser/load acceptance remain open. Existing
messaging, surveys/forms, feedback source integrations, roadmap/changelog and
other original UserFn requirements are not completed by this local evaluator
checkpoint. Dependency gates are feature configuration, not an authorization
boundary replacing server-side access control.
EOF
